title: Extended Basis Sets (Double Zeta and Split-Valence)
lead: The smallest basis gives each atomic orbital one function. Double- and triple-zeta sets give it several functions of different ζ, split-valence sets do so only for the valence orbitals, and Pople's names say how many Gaussians each function holds.
notes: From the book's page under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, curated by Delmar Larsen (LibreTexts), with nothing left out; the double- and triple-zeta exponents in Figure 11.3.1 + 11.3.2 (0.80 and 1.60; 0.60, 1.20 and 2.00) are values chosen to bracket hydrogen's 1.24, not a published basis.
exercise_notes: The book prints no exercises for this section; both exercises and their solutions were written by AI, on counting the functions of Pople basis sets and on the cost of a double-zeta basis. Bloom levels and concept tags were chosen by AI.

figures.original_caption: A "double zeta" basis set with each Atomic Orbital is represented by 2 orbital functions with different ζ values. A "triple zeta" basis with each Atomic Orbital is represented by 3 orbital functions with different ζ values.

exercises.source_id: More examples are shown in Table 11.3.2
exercises.prompt:
Count the orbital functions and the Gaussian primitives of a water molecule, H₂O, in three basis sets. In STO-3G each orbital function of the minimal basis is a contraction of three primitives; for 3-21G and 6-31G use Table 11.3.2.

  1. orbital functions in STO-3G
  2. primitives in STO-3G
  3. orbital functions in 3-21G
  4. primitives in 3-21G
  5. orbital functions in 6-31G
  6. primitives in 6-31G

parts.hint: The minimal basis of oxygen is 1s, 2s and three 2p; each hydrogen has a 1s.

answer.solution:
Oxygen's minimal basis is 1s, 2s and three 2p orbitals, 5 orbital functions, and each hydrogen has one 1s. In STO-3G that makes 5 + 1 + 1 = 7 orbital functions, each from three primitives, so 3 × 7 = 21 primitives.

In 3-21G oxygen, in the Li–Ne row of Table 11.3.2, has 9 orbital functions from 15 primitives, and each hydrogen has 2 from 3: 9 + 2(2) = 13 orbital functions and 15 + 2(3) = 21 primitives.

In 6-31G oxygen has 9 orbital functions from 22 primitives, and each hydrogen 2 from 4: 13 orbital functions and 22 + 2(4) = 30 primitives.

Both split-valence sets nearly double the number of orbital functions, and with it the size of the Hamiltonian matrix. 3-21G does so with no more primitives than STO-3G.

exercises.source_id: there will be about 3–4 times more matrix elements to evaluate
exercises.prompt:
A calculation on a molecule uses a single-zeta basis of $N = 10$ orbital functions. Taking the Hermiticity of the Hamiltonian into account, how many distinct matrix elements $H_{ij}$ must be evaluated

  1. in this basis,
  2. in a double-zeta basis for the same molecule?
  3. By what factor does the number grow?

parts.hint: Since $H_{ji} = H_{ij}^*$, only the diagonal and the elements on one side of it are distinct.

answer.solution:
Because the Hamiltonian is Hermitian, $H_{ji} = H_{ij}^*$, so only the $N$ diagonal elements and the elements above the diagonal need evaluating: $N(N+1)/2 = 10 \times 11/2 = 55$.

The double-zeta basis has $2N = 20$ orbital functions, so $20 \times 21/2 = 210$ distinct elements.

The number grows by $210/55 = 3.82$. That lies between the 3 and 4 the text gives: the factor is $2(2N+1)/(N+1)$, which is 3 at $N = 1$ and approaches 4 as $N$ grows.

footnotes.html: Fluorine's 1s exponent is 8.65 (Clementi and Raimondi's 8.6501), as Table 7.3.1's note gives it; 8.56 swaps two digits.

The third line is the function on atom B, $\ket{\phi_{\text{STO-3G},B}}$. Hehre, Stewart and Pople's third coefficient is 0.44463454, printed 0.44463545. Each primitive also carries its normalization factor $(2\alpha/\pi)^{3/4}$, which the display leaves out: the coefficients belong to normalized Gaussians.
Section 1.5.3.2 is a section of the course this page was taken from; this book has none.
The double-zeta basis is Figure 11.3.1; Figure 11.3.2 is the triple-zeta one.
The orbital functions begin to lose their original meaning as atomic orbitals.
The prize was awarded "for his development of computational methods in quantum chemistry"; the first "for" doubles the citation's own.

The table's header row was lost at the source, and "(l)2-4 (l)5-7 (l)8-10" is left over from its LaTeX rules. The three groups of Contraction, OF and GTO are 3-21G, 6-31G and 6-311G, in that order, as the H–He contractions (3s)→[2s], (4s)→[2s] and (5s)→[3s] show.

The table is scrambled at the source: its first row holds the headings of its columns (polarized, diffuse functions, both), and the other rows repeat names and run to unequal lengths. It lists the families 3-21G, 4-21G, 4-31G, 6-21G, 6-31G and 6-311G, with polarization functions (*), diffuse functions (+) or both (+*), as in 3-21G*, 3-21+G, 3-21+G*, 6-31G*, 6-31+G* and 6-311+G*, and 6-31G(3df, 3pd), which adds three sets of d functions and one of f to the heavy atoms and three of p and one of d to hydrogen. Which name belonged in which cell cannot be recovered.

derivations.what: the cost of a double-zeta basis

assumes.text: A single-zeta basis of $N$ orbital functions gives an $N\times N$ Hamiltonian matrix.

then.why: Of the $N^2$ elements, $N$ lie on the diagonal. Since $H_{ji} = H_{ij}^*$, each element below the diagonal repeats one above it, so only half of the other $N^2 - N$ need evaluating.

assumes.text: A double-zeta basis for the same molecule has $2N$ orbital functions, so its Hamiltonian is a $2N\times 2N$ matrix.

then.why: The count holds for a basis of any size; here $2N$ functions take the place of $N$.

steps.cap: The smallest basis has $N = 1$, where $2/(N+1) = 1$. As $N$ grows, $2/(N+1)$ shrinks toward zero, so the ratio rises from 3 toward 4.
